I have not obtained the requested structural proof, and I have not found a feasible counterexample. I can isolate the missing six-row step quite precisely: a compression statement for a  $6\times4$  extension would give a short two-phase induction. I also obtain a structural signed-boundary inequality for two-row strips, but its boundary terms do not automatically cancel when three strips are joined.There is a separate logical point about your discovery: literal equality of the complete normalized boundary vectors at widths  $6$  and  $8$  already implies all subsequent even widths by the transfer recurrence. That is stronger than checking the terminal optimum through width  $30$ . It supplies an all-length finite certificate, assuming the exact vector equality and transition model, but it does not supply the structural proof you requested.Here are the proved reductions and the exact remaining gap.1. The target is an injection-sized inequality between selected vertices and holesWrite
$$H=V(R)\setminus(T\cup P).$$
Because  $M$  is an actual matching,
$$|P|=2|M|,\qquad |V(R)|=|T|+|P|+|H|=12n.$$
Consequently,
$$2\bigl(|T|+|M|-6n\bigr)=|T|-|H|.$$
Thus the target is exactly
$$\boxed{|T|\le |H|.}$$
Partition the board into the  $3n$  standard  $2\times2$  blocks, and put
$$q(B)=|T\cap B|-|H\cap B|
     =2|T\cap B|+|P\cap B|-4.$$
Then
$$\sum_Bq(B)=|T|-|H|.$$
The local possibilities are very restricted:A block contains at most two selected vertices.If its two selected vertices are adjacent, both other vertices must be holes.If its two selected vertices are diagonal, at most one of the remaining vertices can be occupied.With one selected vertex, a block contains at most two matching endpoints.It follows that
$$q(B)\le1,$$
and the only positive block consists of two diagonal selected vertices, one matching endpoint, and one hole. Its unique matching endpoint must be matched outside the block.The zero-charge blocks containing matching endpoints have only two forms:all four vertices are in  $P$ ;two adjacent vertices are in  $P$ , and the opposite side consists of one selected vertex and one hole.In the latter form, the selected vertex touches exactly one of the two matching endpoints.Two positive blocks cannot be joined directly by their unique endpoints’ matching edge. The selected vertex parallel to that edge in the first block is already adjacent to its own endpoint, so it forces the parallel vertex in the receiving block to be a hole. The positive receiving pattern would place a selected vertex there.This gives the natural charging argument. The difficulty is that the matching route can turn through neutral blocks.2. A proved signed-boundary inequality for two rowsThe following lemma requires neither anchors nor freezing.Two-row signed-boundary lemmaLet  $S$  be a  $2\times2n$  strip inside a larger feasible configuration. Matching edges may leave  $S$  through its top or bottom. Let
$$Q_S=\{p\in P\cap S:\text{the actual mate of }p\text{ lies outside }S\}.$$
There are charges
$$\sigma(p)\in\{-1,0,1\},\qquad p\in P\cap S,$$
depending only on the  $2\times2$  block containing  $p$ , such that
$$\boxed{
|T\cap S|-|H\cap S|
\le \sum_{p\in Q_S}\sigma(p).
}
\tag{1}$$
Use the following assignments. Horizontal and vertical refer to the two-row strip.Contents of a blockCharges on its matching endpointsTwo diagonal  $T$ , one  $P$ , one  $H$  $+1$  on the unique  $P$ One  $T$ , two horizontally adjacent  $P$ , one  $H$  $+1$  on the  $P$  vertically adjacent to  $T$ , and  $-1$  on the other  $P$ One  $T$ , two vertically adjacent  $P$ , one  $H$ Both charges  $0$ Four  $P$ All charges  $0$ Two  $T$ , no  $P$ No chargesNo  $T$ , three  $P$ , one  $H$  $-1$  on the  $P$  vertically adjacent to  $H$ , and  $0$  on the other twoEvery other feasible block $-1$  on each  $P$ ProofFirst, for every block,
$$q(B)\le\sum_{p\in P\cap B}\sigma(p).
\tag{2}$$
This is equality for the positive and neutral types and for the three- $P$  type.For every remaining type, writing  $t=|T\cap B|$  and  $p=|P\cap B|$ , the local classification gives  $t+p\le2$ . Therefore
$$q(B)=2t+p-4\le-p,$$
which proves (2) for the remaining charge assignment.Next, every actual matching edge entirely inside  $S$  has endpoint-charge sum at most zero.Only edges incident to a  $+1$  endpoint need consideration. Such an endpoint has a selected vertex vertically adjacent to it, so its mate cannot be vertically inside the strip.If its mate is in the same block, the block is the horizontal two- $P$  type, and its mate has charge  $-1$ .Otherwise, the matching edge crosses horizontally into the next block. The selected vertex vertically adjacent to the  $+1$  endpoint already has its one occupied neighbour. It therefore forces the parallel vertex of the receiving block to be a hole. The receiving block consequently contains an incoming  $P$  with a hole vertically adjacent to it.The charge at that incoming  $P$  is  $-1$ :in a neutral block, it is the negative endpoint of a horizontal two- $P$  pair;in a three- $P$  block, it is precisely the endpoint vertically adjacent to the hole;in every other possible receiving block, all matching endpoints receive  $-1$ .Thus every internal matching edge incident to a positive charge has sum zero, and every other internal matching edge has nonpositive sum.Summing (2) and grouping internal endpoints by their actual matching edges leaves only the endpoints in  $Q_S$ . This proves (1).  $\square$ ConsequencesFor a closed  $2\times2n$  board,  $Q_S=\varnothing$ , so
$$|T|\le|H|,
\qquad
|T|+|M|\le2n.$$
For the six-row board, this proves the requested bound whenever the actual matching has no edges crossing either of the row-pair cuts
$$2/3,\qquad 4/5.$$
Apply the lemma to rows  $1,2$ , then  $3,4$ , then  $5,6$ .The unrestricted problem requires controlling the signed boundary terms across those two cuts.3. Why simply summing the strip inequalities is insufficientThose signed boundary terms need not cancel.Here is a literal feasible configuration showing the issue. This is not a counterexample to the requested inequality; it is a counterexample to automatic cancellation of the strip boundary terms.On a  $6\times4$  board, take
$$T=\{(1,1),(4,1)\},$$
and
$$P=\{(2,1),(2,2),(3,1),(3,2)\}
\cup\bigl(\{1,2,3,4\}\times\{3,4\}\bigr).$$
All remaining vertices are holes. Use the matching
$$\begin{aligned}
M=\{&
\{(2,1),(3,1)\},
\{(2,2),(2,3)\},
\{(1,3),(1,4)\},\\
&
\{(2,4),(3,4)\},
\{(3,2),(3,3)\},
\{(4,3),(4,4)\}
\}.
\end{aligned}$$
Each selected vertex has exactly one occupied neighbour, and the listed edges are disjoint and cover  $P$ .For the strip charges above:the edge  $(2,1)(3,1)$  crosses the cut  $2/3$  with charge  $+1$  at both endpoints;the other matching edge crossing that cut,  $(2,4)(3,4)$ , has charge  $0$  at both endpoints.Hence the total signed boundary contribution is  $+2$ . It is compensated by two internal horizontal matching edges with charge sum  $-1$  each.Thus a proof cannot discard all negative internal-edge contributions and then assert that the remaining boundary contributions cancel. That loses the compensation needed even in this small feasible example.4. A small candidate boundary potential and one exact missing lemmaThere is a more focused way to formulate the six-row problem than assigning an unexplained value to each of the  $2404$  signatures.For a legal boundary signature  $s=(O,F,R)$ , consider a closed completion appended on its right. It must:supply the actual mates of the pending endpoints in  $R$ ;respect the restrictions imposed by  $O,F$ ;have no pending endpoints at its final boundary.For a completion  $C$  of  $\ell$  columns, define its normalized reward by
$$\operatorname{rew}(C)=2|T_C|+|P_C|-6\ell.$$
Matching endpoints in its first column whose mates are in the preceding prefix are counted once in  $|P_C|$ , as required by your column weight.Define
$$K_0(s)=
\max\left(
\{0:R(s)=0\}
\cup
\{\operatorname{rew}(C):
C\text{ is a legal closed two-column completion of }s\}
\right).
\tag{3}$$
Thus  $K_0$  is defined by an optimization on a twelve-vertex ladder, with the option of stopping immediately when  $R=0$ .For a legal one-column transition  $s\to s'$ , let
$$r(s,s')=w(s,s')-6.$$
Define
$$K_1(s)=\max_{s\to s'}\bigl(r(s,s')+K_0(s')\bigr).
\tag{4}$$
Equivalently,  $K_1$  is the best normalized reward of a closed completion with one or three columns.The candidate prefix potentials are
$$\Phi_0=-K_0,\qquad \Phi_1=-K_1.$$
What is already proved about this candidateWhenever  $R(s)=0$ ,
$$K_0(s)=0.
\tag{5}$$
Indeed, stopping gives reward zero. A two-column completion with no incoming matching endpoints is a closed  $6\times2$  configuration. Rotate it and apply the proved  $2\times6$  ladder theorem: its normalized reward is at most zero. Additional restrictions from the preceding boundary cannot improve that maximum.In particular, the empty initial boundary satisfies
$$\Phi_0(\varnothing)=0.$$
Also, definition (4) immediately gives one transition inequality:
$$r(s,s')+\Phi_1(s)\le\Phi_0(s').
\tag{6}$$
The missing structural statementThe other transition inequality follows from exactly this compression statement:Four-column compression. For every legal six-row boundary  $s$ , every legal closed four-column completion  $C$  satisfies
$$\operatorname{rew}(C)\le K_0(s).
\tag{7}$$
In other words, there exists a legal closed completion using zero or two columns with at least the same normalized reward.Equivalently,
$$K_0(s)\ge
\max_{s\to s'\to s''}
\left(
r(s,s')+r(s',s'')+K_0(s'')
\right).
\tag{8}$$
The two-column alternatives on the right are already included in  $K_0$ ; the new content is the four-column alternative.If (7) were proved structurally, then (8) and (4) would yield
$$r(s,s')+\Phi_0(s)\le\Phi_1(s').
\tag{9}$$
Equations (6) and (9) telescope along every finite configuration. Starting from the empty boundary gives
$$2|T|+|P|-6w
\le\Phi_{w\bmod2}(s_{\rm final}).$$
For even  $w$  and a closed final boundary, (5) makes the right side zero. With  $w=2n$ , this is exactly
$$|T|+|M|\le6n.$$
I have not proved (7). The exact transfer computations support this candidate, but that does not replace the missing geometric argument.There is a specific trap in the most tempting compression: after deleting the last two columns, one might turn the retained mate of a positively charged deleted endpoint from  $P$  into  $T$ . The retained endpoint can have several occupied neighbours in the retained columns. The signed-boundary lemma gives no bound on that degree, so the proposed conversion can be infeasible.5. What full-vector stabilization does implyLet  $v_w(s)$  be the maximum normalized score
$$2|T|+|P|-6w$$
of a legal width- $w$  prefix ending at  $s$ , with value  $-\infty$  for an unreachable signature.Your exact transition rules define a fixed max-plus operator
$$(\mathcal A f)(s')
=
\max_{s\to s'}\bigl(f(s)+w(s,s')-6\bigr),$$
so that
$$v_{w+1}=\mathcal A v_w.$$
If the reported stabilization means the literal identity
$$v_8=v_6$$
on the whole signature space, then
$$v_{6+2k}=v_6\qquad(k\ge0)$$
by induction. The odd equality follows automatically:
$$v_9=\mathcal A v_8=\mathcal A v_6=v_7.$$
Together with the bounds at widths  $2,4,6$ , this establishes every even width through a finite transfer certificate.There is a small initialization detail: the stationary vector  $v_6$  should be used starting at width six. It need not assign zero to the empty boundary, so one cannot silently use it as a potential initialized at width zero. The completion potential in (3), if its compression inequality is proved, avoids that issue.Scope of the result hereThe structural argument above proves the two-row theorem and the six-row case with no matching edges across the two row-pair cuts. It does not establish the unrestricted anchor-free six-row theorem without the finite transfer certificate.The precise unresolved structural obligation is (7), or an equivalent argument controlling matching routes that turn between the three row pairs. No conclusion about coefficient  $1$  for arbitrary even-by-even height follows from these partial arguments.
scope: Structural signed two-row boundary lemma and nonsharp cross-strip cancellation obstruction. No unrestricted structural six-row proof was obtained.
correction: The proposed closed four-to-zero/two-column compression lemma is false: realizable state (54,4,50) has exact short reward -1 but an explicit four-column reward +1. Written classification upper bound and coordinate check are published separately.
